Advantageous lands at first underwent gain and loss, yet were ultimately settled through the private motives of a great state; advantageous lands subsequently underwent gain and loss, yet were ultimately settled through the transforming influence of a sage. For although the gains and losses of the lands west of the Ji and of Wenyang were not the same, how can their return out of private favor compare to the rectitude of their return through the transforming influence of a sage? When we reflect upon the flourishing age of the Western Zhou, the Kingly Way prevailed, rulers were invested with ceremonial茅 grass and enfeoffed with land, and the territories belonging to the various states…

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
者有定制矣爾疆我理而經界之正於諸侯者有常
制矣豈意取予不常得失無定如春秋之世者邪是
故濟西魯之故田也其為曹人之所侵有年矣今也
僖公當國晉文乃申伯討於曹伯班其侵地於諸侯
是田已歸於魯矣異時宣公以不義而得國深懼齊
人之討其罪乃致濟西以賂乎齊而是田又為齊有
焉然昔也恃伯令而得之今也因納賂而失之何至
宣之十年而齊人又舉以歸我邪盖宣公於齊順其
所欲率賦從師殆無虛歲君朝臣聘無有寧日是以
===
齊惠悅其能順事已而以所取濟西之田歸之也春
秋書曰歸我則是舉也出於親愛惠遺之私可知矣
至若汶陽亦魯之故田也其為齊人之利又非一年
矣今也成公在位卻克大戰于鞌以挫强齊袁婁要
盟令反侵地是田已歸於魯矣未幾晉景以姑息而
為政喜齊人之服已而使韓穿來言於魯而是田又
為齊有焉然向也恃伯力而得之今也因伯令而失
之何至定之十年而齊人又以之來歸邪盖定公會
齊侯於夾谷用聖人以相禮文事武備外折其奸詞

punctuated: 者，有定制矣；爾疆我理，而經界之正於諸侯者，有常制矣。豈意取予不常、得失無定，如春秋之世者邪？是故濟西，魯之故田也，其為曹人之所侵有年矣。今也僖公當國，晉文乃申伯討於曹伯，班其侵地於諸侯，是田已歸於魯矣。異時，宣公以不義而得國，深懼齊人之討其罪，乃致濟西以賂乎齊，而是田又為齊有焉。然昔也恃伯令而得之，今也因納賂而失之，何至宣之十年，而齊人又舉以歸我邪？盖宣公於齊，順其所欲，率賦從師，殆無虛歲，君朝臣聘，無有寧日，是以齊惠悅其能順事已，而以所取濟西之田歸之也。《春秋》書曰「歸我」，則是舉也，出於親愛惠遺之私可知矣。至若汶陽，亦魯之故田也，其為齊人之利又非一年矣。今也成公在位，卻克大戰于鞌以挫强齊，袁婁要盟，令反侵地，是田已歸於魯矣。未幾，晉景以姑息而為政，喜齊人之服已，而使韓穿來言於魯，而是田又為齊有焉。然向也恃伯力而得之，今也因伯令而失之，何至定之十年，而齊人又以之來歸邪？盖定公會齊侯於夾谷，用聖人以相禮，文事武備，外折其奸；詞…
translation_en:
… [the lands belonging to the various states] had fixed regulations; with "your boundaries and our divisions," the rectification of borders among the feudal lords had constant rules. Who could have expected that taking and giving would be so inconstant, and gain and loss so unsettled, as in the age of the Spring and Autumn?

Therefore, the lands west of the Ji River (Jixi) were the old fields of Lu, which had been encroached upon by the people of Cao for years. Now, when Duke Xi was in power, Duke Wen of Jin carried out the hegemon's punitive expedition against the Earl of Cao and distributed his encroached lands back to the feudal lords, so these fields had already been returned to Lu. At a later time, Duke Xuan obtained the state through unrighteousness; deeply fearing that the people of Qi would punish his crime, he handed over the lands west of the Ji as a bribe to Qi, and thus these fields once again belonged to Qi. Yet formerly Lu relied on the hegemon's command to gain them, and now because of offering a bribe it lost them—why then, by the tenth year of Duke Xuan, did the people of Qi once again take them and return them to us? Because Duke Xuan complied with whatever Qi desired, leading out levies and following its armies with scarcely an idle year, the ruler paying court visits and ministers making diplomatic inquiries without a day of rest. Therefore Duke Hui of Qi was pleased that he was able to serve him so順 (obediently), and returned to him the fields west of the Ji that he had taken. The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records, "[Qi] returned [the fields] to us," from which it can be known that this act arose from the private favor of affection and generous bestowal.

As for Wenyang, it too was the old fields of Lu, and its serving as a benefit to the people of Qi had also been for more than a year. Now, when Duke Cheng was on the throne,郤克 (Xi Ke) fought a great battle at An to crush powerful Qi, and at Yuanlou forced a covenant ordering the return of encroached lands, so these fields had already been returned to Lu. Before long, Duke Jing of Jin conducted his governance with indulgent appeasement; pleased that the people of Qi had submitted to him, he sent Han Chuan to come and speak to Lu, and thus these fields once again belonged to Qi. Yet previously Lu relied on the hegemon's strength to gain them, and now because of the hegemon's command it lost them—why then, by the tenth year of Duke Ding, did the people of Qi once again come to return them? Because when Duke Ding met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu, he employed the Sage [Confucius] to assist in the rites: with civil affairs and military preparedness, externally he foiled their treachery; with words…

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
嚴誼正内破其詐於是齊景悔罪之不暇而舉是田
以謝過也春秋書曰來歸則是舉也出於願慕感悅
之誠可見矣吁濟西一得一失而終歸於大國之私
汶陽一得一失而終歸於聖人之化然私以相與又
烏可與聖化例論哉抑考讙闡之田亦齊人之歸我
也春秋不例之濟西汶陽之書法何歟蓋讙闡之歸
由於改過遷善之義比之鄆讙龜陰之歸固不可及
方之濟西之出於私者又豈可同日語哉
禮記
===
地載萬物天垂象取財於地取法於天是以尊
天而親地也故教民美報焉
禮恭安

考試官學士高批此篇述造化有功於人人得以盡
其報本之禮詞理俱到允宜高薦
惟造化著生成之功有以資乎民故聖人舉郊社之
禮示以報其本夫禮莫重於郊社造化之生成既有

天而親地也故教民美報焉
===

考試官侍講杜　批〔發明透徹文思春容可取〕

禮示以報其本夫禮莫重於郊社造化之生成既有
punctuated:
嚴誼正，内破其詐。於是齊景悔罪之不暇，而舉是田以謝過也。《春秋》書曰「來歸」，則是舉也，出於願慕感悅之誠可見矣。吁！濟西一得一失，而終歸於大國之私；汶陽一得一失，而終歸於聖人之化。然私以相與，又烏可與聖化例論哉？抑考讙、闡之田，亦齊人之歸我也，《春秋》不例之濟西、汶陽之書法，何歟？蓋讙、闡之歸，由於改過遷善之義，比之鄆、讙、龜陰之歸固不可及，方之濟西之出於私者，又豈可同日語哉！

《禮記》
「地載萬物，天垂象，取財於地，取法於天，是以尊天而親地也，故教民美報焉。」
禮恭安

惟造化著生成之功，有以資乎民，故聖人舉郊社之禮，示以報其本。夫禮莫重於郊社，造化之生成既有

… stern words and upright righteousness broke their deceit within. Thereupon Duke Jing of Qi had barely time to repent of his offenses, and offered up these lands in apology for his faults. That the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records it as "came to restore [to us]" shows clearly that this act sprang from sincere admiration and heartfelt gladness. Alas! The lands west of the Ji River were once gained and once lost, and in the end were restored out of the private partiality of a great state; the lands of Wenyang were once gained and once lost, and in the end were restored through the transforming influence of a sage. Yet how can mutual giving out of private partiality be discussed in the same breath as the transforming influence of a sage? Moreover, if we examine the lands of Huan and Chan, which the people of Qi also restored to us, why did the Spring and Autumn Annals not treat them according to the historiographical formula used for the lands west of the Ji and for Wenyang? Because the restoration of Huan and Chan arose from the righteousness of reforming faults and moving toward the good; while it certainly cannot match the restoration of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin, how could it be spoken of on the same day as the restoration of the lands west of the Ji, which sprang from private partiality!

Record of Rites (Liji)
"The earth supports the myriad things, and heaven suspends its images; resources are taken from the earth, and models are taken from heaven. Therefore one reveres heaven and feels close affection for the earth, and thus teaches the people to make noble recompense."
Li Gong'an 禮恭安 [? likely a transcription error for the candidate's name and native place]

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
功於民聖人安得不示以報功之道哉今夫隤然在
下者地也地以載物為功而萬物散殊類聚群分無
一不載焉穹然在上者天也天以覆物為功而三光
照臨懸象著明無一不繫焉夫地之載物非徒載也
無非為人之所取故器用服食之需養生送死之具
莫不藉以為用焉天之覆物非徒覆也無非為人之
所法故耕作播種之時收穫早晚之候莫不視以為
法焉天地之有功於民也如此可不知致其報乎故
冬至之日祭天於圜丘尊之為甚隆誠以天遠於人
===
取法則有教詔之義父道也故尊之而不親夏至之
日祀地於方澤親之為甚至誠以地近於人取利則
有養育之意母道也故親之而不尊聖人所以尊天
而親地者豈有他哉盖欲使民知天有父之尊而不
敢慢知地有母之親而不敢忽謂之教民美報信乎
有以美善其報之之禮矣大抵此章首言社所以祭
地是獨以社為言至此又以郊禮而並言之者盖物
非天不生非地不成其功一而已矣故社雖以天為
對而實重於社下文天子大社於國卿大夫祭土神

punctuated: 功於民，聖人安得不示以報功之道哉？今夫隤然在下者，地也。地以載物為功，而萬物散殊，類聚群分，無一不載焉。穹然在上者，天也。天以覆物為功，而三光照臨，懸象著明，無一不繫焉。夫地之載物，非徒載也，無非為人之所取；故器用服食之需，養生送死之具，莫不藉以為用焉。天之覆物，非徒覆也，無非為人之所法；故耕作播種之時，收穫早晚之候，莫不視以為法焉。天地之有功於民也如此，可不知致其報乎？故冬至之日，祭天於圜丘，尊之為甚隆，誠以天遠於人，取法則有教詔之義，父道也，故尊之而不親。夏至之日，祀地於方澤，親之為甚至，誠以地近於人，取利則有養育之意，母道也，故親之而不尊。聖人所以尊天而親地者，豈有他哉？盖欲使民知天有父之尊而不敢慢，知地有母之親而不敢忽。謂之「教民美報」，信乎有以美善其報之之禮矣。大抵此章首言社所以祭地，是獨以社為言；至此又以郊禮而並言之者，盖物非天不生，非地不成，其功一而已矣。故社雖以天為對，而實重於社，下文天子大社於國，卿大夫祭土神
translation_en: …meritorious service to the people, how could the sages not demonstrate the way to repay that merit? Now, that which lies proselytely below is Earth. Earth takes supporting things as its merit; the myriad things in their diverse forms, gathered by kind and divided by group, are every one of them supported by it. That which arches high above is Heaven. Heaven takes sheltering things as its merit; the three luminaries shining down, the suspended images clearly manifest, are every one of them attached to it. Now Earth's supporting of things is not merely supporting them; it is all so that people may draw from them. Therefore, the necessities of utensils, clothing, and food, and the wherewithal for nourishing the living and burying the dead, all rely on it for their use. Heaven's sheltering of things is not merely sheltering them; it is all so that people may take it as a model. Therefore, the times for plowing and sowing, and the early and late seasons for harvesting, are all determined by observing it as a model. Since the merit of Heaven and Earth toward the people is such as this, how could one not know to offer them repayment? Therefore, on the day of the winter solstice, one sacrifices to Heaven at the Round Mound, revering it with the utmost solemnity. Truly, because Heaven is distant from human beings, taking it as a model carries the meaning of instruction and command, which is the way of a father; therefore one reveres it without being intimate with it. On the day of the summer solstice, one sacrifices to Earth at the Square Pool, feeling intimacy toward it to the utmost degree. Truly, because Earth is close to human beings, drawing benefit from it carries the meaning of nurturing and rearing, which is the way of a mother; therefore one is intimate with it without revering it as distant. Why did the sages revere Heaven and feel intimacy toward Earth? Was there any other reason? It was simply that they wished to make the people know that Heaven has the尊 (dignity) of a father and thus not dare to be disrespectful, and know that Earth has the intimacy of a mother and thus not dare to be neglectful. Calling this "teaching the people fine repayment," truly there is that by which the rites of repaying them are made fine and good! In general, this chapter first speaks of the altar of the soil as the means of sacrificing to Earth, speaking solely of the altar of the soil; that it comes at this point to speak of the suburban sacrifice alongside it is because without Heaven things are not born, and without Earth things are not completed—their merit is one and the same. Therefore, although the altar of the soil is paired with Heaven, the emphasis here actually falls on the altar of the soil, as may be seen below in the Son of Heaven establishing the Great Altar of the Soil in the state and the Grandees sacrificing to the spirit of the soil…

text:
於中庸可見學者察諸
德者性之端也樂者德之華也金石絲竹樂之
器也詩言其志也歌咏其聲也舞動其容也
三者本於心然後樂器從之
謝琚

異衆作故特表之
考試官侍講杜批講析詳明文理可觀一結尤佳
考試官學士高批此篇文有發越蓋嘗熟於禮者
===

德性之蘊於中者樂之本聲容之見於外者樂之文
也非本之充積於中安能致文之著見於外哉今夫
樂之為樂由人心而生也性者吾心所具之理德者
得是理於心不失者也德根於性和順積中純然粹
然猶物在中而緒見於外也非德者性之端乎樂以

知樂之理有本而有文，則知樂之作由中而及外。夫德性之蘊於中者，樂之本；聲容之見於外者，樂之文也。非本之充積於中，安能致文之著見於外哉？今夫樂之為樂，由人心而生也。性者，吾心所具之理；德者，得是理於心不失者也。德根於性，和順積中，純然粹然，猶物在中而緒見於外也，非「德者，性之端」乎？樂以章德，英華發外，可嘉可樂，猶金玉之光輝不可掩也，非「樂者，德之華」乎？由是為之金石，則有鍾磬以宣其聲焉；為之絲竹，則有琴瑟以和其音焉，所謂「樂之器」
translation_en:
… at the inner gate, as can be seen from this. Let scholars examine it closely.

"Virtue is the sprout of human nature; music is the flowering of virtue; metal, stone, silk, and bamboo are the instruments of music. Poetry expresses its intent, song chants its voice, and dance moves its demeanor. These three originate in the mind, and only then do the musical instruments follow them."

Xie Ju 謝琚
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Chen 陳: This essay is able to thoroughly integrate the meaning of the topic into its composition, standing far apart from the crowd of other works; therefore it is specially singled out for praise.
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-Waiting Du 杜: The analysis and exposition are detailed and clear, the literary structure is admirable, and the concluding section is especially fine.
Comment by Examiner Academician Gao 高: This essay possesses spirited brilliance; the author is surely one well-versed in the Record of Rites (Liji).

When one understands that the principle of music has both a root and outer refinement, one understands that the creation of music proceeds from the interior and reaches the exterior. Now, moral nature stored within is the root of music; sound and demeanor manifested without are the outer refinement of music. Unless the root is abundantly accumulated within, how could it bring about the clear manifestation of refinement without? Now then, music as music arises from the human mind. Human nature is the principle endowed in our mind; virtue is the obtaining of this principle in the mind without losing it. Virtue is rooted in human nature; harmony and compliance accumulate within, pure and unadulterated, just like an object inside whose thread-end appears on the outside—is this not "virtue is the sprout of human nature"? Music serves to make virtue illustrious; itssplendid flowering issues forth on the outside, worthy of praise and delight, just like the brilliance of gold and jade that cannot be concealed—is this not "music is the flowering of virtue"? From this, when metal and stone are fashioned for it, there are bells and chimes to proclaim its sound; when silk and bamboo are fashioned for it, there are zithers to harmonize its tones—this is what is called "the instruments of music"…

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
也樂之有本有文如此而樂之作寧不由中而達外
乎故在心為志發言為詩志動於內必形於詩以達
其志意焉言之不足故永歌之以發其聲音焉永歌
之不足不知手之舞之足之蹈之以動其容儀焉詩
言其志也歌咏心之聲也舞動心之容也三者皆
□□乎感物而動然後被之八音之器飾以干戚
羽毛之物翕如純如而無相奪倫皦如繹如而纍
乎其如貫從之可知矣故曰知樂之理有本而
有文則知樂之作由中而及外者其以此歟大抵樂
之為樂不外平和順之理而已記曰樂者天地之和
是天地積其氣之和順而無聲之樂已具又曰樂者
聖人之所樂是聖人積德性之和順而有聲之樂始
作有積者必有發有體者必有用非徒以聲音為也
故曰唯樂不可以偽為吁體用一原顯微無間非深
明樂記之旨者孰能識之
論
舜為法於天下

punctuated:
也。樂之有本有文如此，而樂之作，寧不由中而達外乎？故在心為志，發言為詩。志動於內，必形於詩，以達其志意焉；言之不足，故永歌之，以發其聲音焉；永歌之不足，不知手之舞之、足之蹈之，以動其容儀焉。詩言其志也，歌咏心之聲也，舞動心之容也。三者皆□□乎感物而動，然後被之八音之器，飾以干戚羽毛之物，翕如、純如而無相奪倫，皦如、繹如而纍乎其如貫，從之可知矣。故曰：「知樂之理有本而有文，則知樂之作由中而及外者」，其以此歟！大抵樂之為樂，不外平和順之理而已。《記》曰：「樂者，天地之和。」是天地積其氣之和順，而無聲之樂已具。又曰：「樂者，聖人之所樂。」是聖人積德性之和順，而有聲之樂始作。有積者必有發，有體者必有用，非徒以聲音為也。故曰：「唯樂不可以偽為。」吁！體用一原，顯微無間，非深明《樂記》之旨者，孰能識之！

論
舜為法於天下
translation_en:
… That music has both root and pattern is thus; how then could the creation of music not proceed from the inside to reach the outside? Therefore, what is in the mind is intent, and when expressed in words, it is poetry. When intent is stirred within, it necessarily takes form in poetry so as to convey one's intent and meaning; when words are insufficient, one draws them out in song so as to give forth their sounds and tones; when drawing them out in song is insufficient, unconsciously the hands dance it and the feet stamp it so as to set in motion one's bearing and deportment. Poetry expresses the intent, song chants the voice of the mind, and dance moves the demeanor of the mind. All three [are rooted in the mind?], stirred by contact with things, and only afterwards are they set to the instruments of the eight timbres and adorned with shields, battle-axes, feathers, and yak-tails—blending harmoniously and purely without encroaching upon one another's order, clear and continuous like pearls strung together—as can be known when it is played out. Therefore it is said: "When one understands that the principle of music has both root and pattern, one understands that the creation of music proceeds from the inside to reach the outside"—is it not for this reason?

In general, music as music is nothing other than the principle of harmony and顺 (accord) [note: 平 is a woodblock print variant for 乎, "nothing other than the principle of harmony and accord"]. The Record of Music (Yueji) says: "Music is the harmony of Heaven and Earth." This means that Heaven and Earth accumulate the harmony and accord of their vital energy (qi), and soundless music is already complete. It also says: "Music is that in which the sages take joy." This means that the sages accumulate the harmony and accord of their moral nature, and only then does music with sound arise. Where there is accumulation, there must be manifestation; where there is substance, there must be function—it is not merely a matter of sounds and tones. Therefore it is said: "Only music cannot be falsified." Ah! Substance and function have a single source, and the manifest and the subtle have no gap between them; who could recognize this without deeply understanding the purport of the Record of Music?

Discourse

"Shun Was a Model for the World"

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
同考試官脩撰裴批孟子此章大段論君子待人者恕
責己者嚴皆不外以仁禮存心也雖舜為法於天下
可傳於後世亦原於此場中立說多涉於規矩方員之至
聖人人倫之至於是罕能發明此作独本仁禮融會成
文非實學不能到故表而出之
考試官侍講杜批文詞整潔筆力滂沛必蓄學之士也
考試官學士高批論本乎仁禮最是
論曰人性莫大於仁也君子以仁存心不過能愛人
而已而未能為法於天下後世焉人性莫大於禮也
===
君子以禮存心亦不過能敬人而已而未能為法於
天下後世焉求其足以為法於天下可傳於後世者
必首出庶物能盡其性者之聖人然後為能然也使
其不能盡所性之全極人倫之道雖欲為法於一人
且不可況可為法於天下乎雖欲為法於天下且未
能況能為法於後世乎愚嘗讀孟軻氏之言而竊疑
之天下之大兆民之廣孰無所性之全也孰無人倫
之道也何獨舜為法於天下可傳於後世乎殊不知
天之生物必厚於人天之生人必厚於聖人人也者

論曰：人性莫大於仁也，君子以仁存心，不過能愛人而已，而未能為法於天下後世焉；人性莫大於禮也，君子以禮存心，亦不過能敬人而已，而未能為法於天下後世焉。求其足以為法於天下、可傳於後世者，必首出庶物、能盡其性者之聖人，然後為能然也。使其不能盡所性之全、極人倫之道，雖欲為法於一人且不可，況可為法於天下乎？雖欲為法於天下且未能，況能為法於後世乎？愚嘗讀孟軻氏之言而竊疑之：天下之大，兆民之廣，孰無所性之全也？孰無人倫之道也？何獨舜為法於天下、可傳於後世乎？殊不知天之生物，必厚於人；天之生人，必厚於聖人。人也者，…

Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Pei: This chapter of the Mencius (Mengzi) broadly discusses how the gentleman is forgiving in dealing with others and strict in making demands of himself—all of which comes down to nothing other than preserving his mind with benevolence and propriety. Even the statement that "Shun was a model for all under Heaven that could be transmitted to later generations" also originates from this. In the examination hall, most arguments wandered into "the compass and square are the perfection of squares and circles; the sage is the perfection of human relationships," and thus few were able to elucidate the true meaning. This essay alone takes benevolence and propriety as its foundation, blending them into a coherent composition. Without solid learning, one could not reach this level; therefore I have singled it out for distinction.

Comment by Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting Du: The diction is neat and pure, and the brushwork is vigorous and abundant; he must be a scholar of accumulated learning.

Comment by Examiner and Academician Gao: Basing the discourse on benevolence and propriety is most apt.

The discourse reads: Nothing in human nature is greater than benevolence. Yet when the gentleman preserves his mind with benevolence, he is merely able to love others and nothing more; he is not yet able to serve as a model for all under Heaven and later generations. Nothing in human nature is greater than propriety. Yet when the gentleman preserves his mind with propriety, he too is merely able to respect others and nothing more; he is not yet able to serve as a model for all under Heaven and later generations. If we seek one who is sufficient to serve as a model for all under Heaven and be transmitted to later generations, it must be a sage who rises preeminent above the multitude of things and is able to fully realize his nature—only then can he be so. Supposing he were unable to exhaust the entirety of his endowed nature and reach the ultimate standard of human relationships, even if he wished to be a model for a single person it would be impossible—how much less could he be a model for all under Heaven? Even if he wished to be a model for all under Heaven he would not yet be able—how much less could he be a model for later generations? I once read the words of Mencius (Meng Ke 孟軻) and privately wondered about them: in the vastness of all under Heaven and the multitude of the millions of people, who does not possess the entirety of his endowed nature? Who does not possess the Way of human relationships? Why was Shun alone a model for all under Heaven that could be transmitted to later generations? Little did I realize that when Heaven gives birth to things, it necessarily favors human beings; and when Heaven gives birth to human beings, it necessarily favors the sages. Human beings…

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
物之至者也聖也者人之至者也舜為人之至而為
聖人夫何不能全其所性而盡其人倫乎觀其濬哲
文明温恭允塞仁極仁不必存養而無念慮之違乎
仁禮極禮不必操存而無纖芥之悖夫禮所謂居天
下之廣居者是也所謂立天下之正位者是也惟其
能盡乎仁義之性是以見於人倫之間者莫非仁禮
之流行彼其父頑至難事也舜盡仁禮以事之而致
其底豫是其父子足以為法於天下焉弟傲至難處
也舜以仁禮處之致其和諧是其兄弟足以為法於
===

臣者豈不足以為天下之法乎二女果若固有之其

Since Shun 舜 was the culmination of mankind and was a sage, how could he be unable to perfect the nature with which he was endowed and fulfill human moral relationships to the utmost? Observe how he was profoundly wise, accomplished, and enlightened, gentle, reverent, and sincerely upright; his benevolence reached the utmost of benevolence, having no need of deliberate preservation and nourishment, yet without a single thought or reflection departing from benevolence; his propriety reached the utmost of propriety, having no need of deliberate grasping and retention, yet without the slightest particle contradicting propriety. This is what is meant by "dwelling in the wide house of the world"; this is what is meant by "standing in the correct seat of the world." Because he was able to fulfill the nature of benevolence and righteousness to the utmost, what was manifested among his human relationships was nothing less than the free flow of benevolence and propriety. Now, his father was obstinately unprincipled and most difficult to serve, yet Shun exhausted benevolence and propriety in serving him and brought him to eventual delight—thus in the relation of father and son he was sufficient to serve as a model for the world. His younger brother was arrogant and most difficult to get along with, yet Shun dealt with him through benevolence and propriety and brought about harmony—thus in the relation of elder and younger brother he was sufficient to serve as a model for the world. Coming to his general supervision of all offices and finally receiving the abdication from Yao 堯, how could the manifestation of his benevolence and propriety in the relation of ruler and minister not be sufficient to serve as a model for the world? With the two daughters of Yao attending on him as if he had always possessed such station, how could the manifestation of his benevolence and propriety in the relation of husband and wife also not be sufficient to serve as a model for the world? Yet not only did the world of his own time take him as a model, but throughout ten thousand generations in the world, among those who are fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, elder and younger brothers, and husbands and wives, there are none who do not also take him as a model; and not only do ten thousand generations in the world take him as a model, but throughout a hundred million generations in the world, among those who are fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, elder and younger brothers, and husbands and wives, there are none who do not take him as a model. This is what is meant by "the Sovereign establishing his supreme standard"; this is what is meant by "regulating the great invariable relations of the world." …different [in distance], what they share in common is this mind and this principle; and although ages differ as to antiquity and the present, what they share in common is also this mind and this principle. Shun fulfilled to the utmost what is common to human minds in order to serve as a model for the world and for future generations. Thus the sageliness of Emperor Shun was not merely that of a sage for a single generation, whom ten thousand generations regard as the supreme sage; nor was he only a sage for ten thousand generations, for there is none among a hundred million generations that does not regard him as the supreme sage. Great indeed is the sageliness of Emperor Shun! Was he not the very ultimate of human relationships? Was he not the standard for the world and for future generations? Alas! Since antiquity all the sages have been sufficient to serve as models for the world; why then does Mencius attribute this solely to Shun, if not because the other sages dealt with the normal state of human relationships, whereas Emperor Shun dealt with the extremity of human relationships? Alas! Emperor Shun is distant now and can no longer be seen. Yet at this very time, a Sage sits on high, fulfilling the entirety of his endowed nature and reaching the utmost greatness of human relationships. Succeeding Heaven and establishing the supreme standard, he suffices to be a teacher and exemplar to the myriad states; handing down instruction and establishing patterns, he suffices to serve as a norm and model for a hundred generations. How fortunate am I, in my simplicity, to witness this in person! Such is my discourse.

…As the Sagely Emperor ascends the throne, all under heaven is moistened by boundless grace; as the creative forces of nature manifest auspicious signs, the Sovereign Earth responds with supreme harmony. Joy surges through court and countryside, and delight overflows among officials and commoners.

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses a mind identical to that of Yao and Shun, and virtue matching that of Yu and Tang. Your Way continues the orthodox succession of a thousand years, and Your enterprise transmits the grand plans of the Four Sagely Ancestors. Holding that the imperial person is the source of all transformations, You daily attend the Classics Colloquium (jingyan) to expound the Way; holding that action is the root of the myriad affairs of state, You open the Hall of Distinction (mingtang) early in the morning to attend to governance. Though it is because You Yourself are rectified that all things are rectified, this also means that when physical form is harmonious, the vital ether is harmonious.

Looking upon this gushing forth of the sweet spring, it is truly the culmination of transformative governance. Sweet as malt-sugar and lustrous as jade, how could it rely on the flavor of clarified butter? Rich in color and crisp in fragrance, what need has it for the work of yeast and malt? Its pureness and clarity are no different from newly brewed wine; its aromatic fragrance truly resembles the yellow libation poured from a jade ladle. It can be offered to the Lord on High to respond to His presence at the Round Mound (Huanqiu), and it can be used to toast the longevity of the Palace of Maternal Munificence (Cigong), bringing a smile to Her face within the kingfisher curtains. Heaven and Earth extend their blessings, having once presented this fine gift in a former reign; seas and mountains display their numinous power, repeatedly manifesting auspicious omens today. Your servant unworthily holds an office in the pure ranks and has personally encountered this grand event. text:
以裨於世教者不其大乎然陰隲莫先於仁厚孝行
莫難於感格請以陰隲之書言之如于公與守爭孝
婦之寃盛吉遇斷囚而垂泣救人坐免者曹褒也守
正不阿者史弼也不寃著稱者非唐臨乎詳審獲報
者非嚴讜乎他如孜孜申理詿誤仁恕如張釋之者
則又有若狄仁傑徐有功者焉是數人者非仁厚之
陰隲者乎以事實之書言之大而感天地動鬼神則
有若阮卓之息風許伯會之感雨者矣又有若王崇
之止雹何琦之滅火者矣微而化強暴格鳥獸孚草
===
木則有若劉平之感盜江革之全難者焉有若蕭放
之致烏蔡邕之異木連理九齡之祥應賈循之致瑞
者焉是數人者非孝行之感格者乎然二書所載大
略如此而二書之旨則各有所在也為善之書非在
於紀述之多在所以導人以至於善而已孝順之書
非在於該載之廣在所以勉人以盡乎孝而已分而
言之雖有不同捻而論之其有裨於世教也信乎其
一致矣於戲盛哉愚生佩服有年姑以是而復明問
之萬一云

正不阿者史弼也不寃著稱者非唐臨乎詳審獲報
者非嚴譔乎他如孜孜卑理註誤仁恕如張釋之者
則又有若狄仁傑徐有功者焉是數人者非仁厚之
陰騭者乎以事實之書言之大而感天地動鬼神則
有若阮卓之息風許伯會之感雨者矣又有若王崇
之止雹何琦之滅火者矣微而化強暴格鳥獸孚草
===
木則有若劉平之感盗江革之全難者焉有若蕭放
之致烏蔡邕之異木連理九齡之祥應貫循之致瑞
者焉是數人者非孝行之感格者乎然二書所載大
略如此而二書之旨則各有所在也爲善之書非在
於紀述之多在所以導人以至於善而已孝順之書
非在於該載之廣在所以勉人以盡乎孝而已分而
□之雖有不同總而論之其有裨於世教也信乎其
□致矣於戲盛哉愚生佩服有年始以是而復明問
punctuated: 以裨於世教者，不其大乎！然陰隲莫先於仁厚，孝行莫難於感格。請以《陰隲》之書言之：如于公與守爭孝婦之寃，盛吉遇斷囚而垂泣；救人坐免者，曹褒也；守正不阿者，史弼也；不寃著稱者，非唐臨乎？詳審獲報者，非嚴讜乎？他如孜孜申理詿誤、仁恕如張釋之者，則又有若狄仁傑、徐有功者焉。是數人者，非仁厚之陰隲者乎？以《事實》之書言之：大而感天地、動鬼神，則有若阮卓之息風、許伯會之感雨者矣；又有若王崇之止雹、何琦之滅火者矣。微而化強暴、格鳥獸、孚草木，則有若劉平之感盜、江革之全難者焉；有若蕭放之致烏、蔡邕之異木連理、九齡之祥應、賈循之致瑞者焉。是數人者，非孝行之感格者乎？然二書所載，大略如此，而二書之旨，則各有所在也。為善之書，非在於紀述之多，在所以導人以至於善而已；孝順之書，非在於該載之廣，在所以勉人以盡乎孝而已。分而言之，雖有不同；捻而論之，其有裨於世教也，信乎其一致矣。於戲盛哉！愚生佩服有年，姑以是而復明問之萬一云。
translation_en:
…is not that by which they benefit the moral instruction of the age great indeed! Yet in secret virtue (yinzhi), nothing comes before benevolence and generosity; in filial conduct, nothing is more difficult than moving and reaching [Heaven and things]. Allow me to speak of this through the book on Secret Virtue (Weishan yinzhi): for instance, Yu Gong 于公 argued with the Grand Administrator over the injustice done to a filial wife, and Sheng Ji 盛吉 wept whenever he had to pass judgment on prisoners. He who saved others and was consequently dismissed from office was Cao Bao 曹褒; he who upheld rectitude without flattery was Shi Bi 史弼. Was it not Tang Lin 唐臨 who became renowned for inflicting no冤 [injustices]? Was it not Yan Dang 嚴讜 who received recompense for his meticulousness in trials? As for others who tirelessly redressed the grievances of those implicated by error and showed benevolence and leniency like Zhang Shizhi 張釋之, there were also men such as Di Renjie 狄仁傑 and Xu Yougong 徐有功. Were not these several men exemplars of secret virtue through benevolence and generosity?

To speak of it through the book on Factual Accounts [of Filial Piety] (Xiaoshun shishi): on a grand scale, in moving Heaven and Earth and stirring ghosts and spirits, there were men such as Ruan Zhuo 阮卓, who calmed the wind, and Xu Bohui 許伯會, who moved [Heaven] to rain; and there were also men such as Wang Chong 王崇, who stopped the hail, and He Qi 何琦, who extinguished the fire. On a subtler scale, in transforming the violent, reaching birds and beasts, and inspiring plants and trees, there were men such as Liu Ping 劉平, who moved bandits, and Jiang Ge 江革, who preserved [his mother] through calamity; and there were men such as Xiao Fang 蕭放, who attracted [auspicious] crows, Cai Yong 蔡邕, for whom marvelous trees grew with intertwined branches, [Zhang] Jiuling 張九齡, who met with auspicious responses, and Jia Xun 賈循, who brought forth felicitous omens. Were not these several men exemplars of moving and reaching through filial conduct?

Such, in general outline, is what is recorded in the two books; yet the purport of each of the two books has its own focus. The book on doing good does not lie in the abundance of its records, but simply in that by which it guides people to arrive at goodness; the book on filial obedience does not lie in the breadth of its coverage, but simply in that by which it encourages people to exhaust their filial piety. Spoken of separately, although they differ, when taken together [reading 捻 as 總] and discussed, in benefiting the moral instruction of the age they are truly one and the same! Oh, how magnificent! I, a foolish student, have cherished and admired them for years, and tentatively offer this in reply to one ten-thousandth of Your enlightened inquiry.

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
語史記漢書尤未能一に合安敢與尚書春秋例而論
邪宋大儒司馬溫公以歷代史籍煩多易紀傳為編
年作資治通鑑一書其文約其事備固足以為古今
之勸戒惜其不本春秋之法而失褒貶之公觀夫黜
昭烈而僭曹魏黜中宗而紀武后非刪述之有可議
者乎謂四皓翼太子則以為子制父謂姚崇十書則
以為臣要君又非瑕疵之有可指者乎此其不能不
待於朱子綱目之作也夫歷代皆史也於兩漢晋隋
則曰書於三國則曰志於南北五代則曰史其名雖
===
有曰書曰志曰史之不同而所以寓褒貶之意則同
也孟子曰晋之乘楚之檮杌魯之春秋其義一也良
有以夫吁作史無定論本之春秋有定論考史無定
法本之春秋有定法以春秋之法而觀歷代之史則
其褒貶去取立論是非有不待辨而明矣愚也於歷
代之史未能博識而精究之今因明問姑述所聞以
對惟執事以為何如

第三問
punctuated:
語《史記》、《漢書》，尤未能一に合，安敢與《尚書》、《春秋》例而論邪？宋大儒司馬溫公以歷代史籍煩多，易紀傳為編年，作《資治通鑑》一書。其文約，其事備，固足以為古今之勸戒；惜其不本《春秋》之法，而失褒貶之公。觀夫黜昭烈而僭曹魏，黜中宗而紀武后，非刪述之有可議者乎？謂四皓翼太子，則以為子制父；謂姚崇十書，則以為臣要君，又非瑕疵之有可指者乎？此其不能不待於朱子《綱目》之作也。夫歷代皆史也，於兩漢、晋、隋則曰《書》，於三國則曰《志》，於南北、五代則曰《史》。其名雖有曰《書》、曰《志》、曰《史》之不同，而所以寓褒貶之意則同也。孟子曰：「晋之《乘》，楚之《檮杌》，魯之《春秋》，其義一也。」良有以夫！吁！作史無定論，本之《春秋》有定論；考史無定法，本之《春秋》有定法。以《春秋》之法而觀歷代之史，則其褒貶去取、立論是非，有不待辨而明矣。愚也於歷代之史，未能博識而精究之，今因明問，姑述所聞以對，惟執事以為何如。
第三問
translation_en:
…speaking of the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) and the History of the Former Han (Hanshu), it is even less able to tally with them point by point—how then could one dare to discuss it on a par with the Book of Documents (Shangshu) and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)?

In the Song dynasty, the great Confucian scholar Sima Wengong [Sima Guang 司馬光], considering the historical records of successive dynasties to be voluminous and繁雜 [numerous], changed the annals-biography format into a chronological one and composed the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian). Its wording is concise and its coverage of events complete, which is indeed sufficient to serve as encouragement and warning for past and present. Yet it is a pity that he did not base himself on the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals, and thus lost impartiality in praise and blame. Look at how he relegated Zhaolie [Liu Bei 劉備 of Shu-Han] and accorded legitimacy to the usurping Cao-Wei, or how he relegated Emperor Zhongzong [of Tang] and placed Empress Wu in the basic annals—are these not aspects of his editing and narration that are open to criticism? When speaking of the Four Hoaryheads supporting the Crown Prince [of Han], he deemed it a son controlling his father; when speaking of Yao Chong's 姚崇 ten-point memorial [submitted to Emperor Xuanzong of Tang], he deemed it a subject coercing his ruler—are these not also flaws that can be pointed out? This is why it could not but await the composition of Master Zhu's [Zhu Xi 朱熹] Outline and Details (Gangmu [Zizhi tongjian gangmu]).

Now, all the successive dynasties have their histories: for the Two Han, Jin, and Sui, they are called "Books" (Shu); for the Three Kingdoms, they are called "Records" (Zhi); for the Southern and Northern Dynasties and the Five Dynasties, they are called "Histories" (Shi). Although their titles differ in being called Books, Records, or Histories, the intention of lodging praise and blame within them is the same. Mencius said: "The Sheng of Jin, the Taowu of Chu, and the Chunqiu of Lu are one and the same in their significance." There is truly good reason for this!

Alas! In writing history there is no fixed judgment, but when based on the Spring and Autumn Annals, there is a fixed judgment; in examining history there is no fixed method, but when based on the Spring and Autumn Annals, there is a fixed method. If one views the histories of successive dynasties through the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals, then their praise and blame, their selection and rejection, and the right and wrong of their arguments become clear without waiting for debate. Ignorant as I am, I have not been able to acquire broad knowledge of or thoroughly investigate the histories of successive dynasties. Now, in response to your enlightened question, I tentatively state what I have heard by way of reply, and only ask what Your Excellency thinks of it.

The Third Question

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
同考試官教諭林批有考據有断制策塲之尤者可嘉
考試官侍講杜批隨問隨答鑿鑿有條足見博學
考試官學士高批考究精詳可取
為治莫大於作樂作樂莫先於律呂律呂者聲樂之
本也作樂而不以律呂則何以和其高下長短之節而
使之無乖戾凌犯之失哉知此則可復明問之萬一
矣昔者吾夫子以天縱之聖當春秋之時慨音樂之
廢缺因當時之樂官而語之以樂乃以翕如純如皦
如繹如為一成孟子學孔子者論樂之大成則曰金
===
聲而玉振之似有不同然就其中而論之則翕純皦
繹而非金以宣其聲於始玉以收其韵於終固不足
為樂之一成苟金聲玉振而不能翕純皦繹則又何
以為樂之和哉若夫孟子謂不以六律不能正五音
何夫子語魯大師之樂乃不舉六律者蓋樂由六律
而後和苟至於翕純皦繹之和未有不由於六律者
也故雖不明言夫六律而六律在其中矣若以三統
言之則黃鍾為天統太簇為地統姑洗為人統是也
以配十二月言之則黃鍾属子大呂属丑太簇属寅

為治莫大於作樂，作樂莫先於律呂，律呂者，聲樂之本也。作樂而不以律呂，則何以和其高下長短之節，而使之無乖戾凌犯之失哉？知此則可復明問之萬一矣。昔者吾夫子以天縱之聖，當春秋之時，慨音樂之廢缺，因當時之樂官而語之以樂，乃以「翕如、純如、皦如、繹如」為一成；孟子學孔子者，論樂之大成，則曰「金聲而玉振之」，似有不同。然就其中而論之，則翕、純、皦、繹，而非金以宣其聲於始，玉以收其韵於終，固不足為樂之一成；苟金聲玉振，而不能翕、純、皦、繹，則又何以為樂之和哉？若夫孟子謂「不以六律，不能正五音」，何夫子語魯大師之樂，乃不舉六律者？蓋樂由六律而後和，苟至於翕、純、皦、繹之和，未有不由於六律者也。故雖不明言夫六律，而六律在其中矣。若以三統言之，則黃鍾為天統，太簇為地統，姑洗為人統，是也。以配十二月言之，則黃鍾属子，大呂属丑，太簇属寅，

In governing, nothing is greater than instituting music, and in instituting music, nothing takes precedence over the yang and yin pitch-pipes (lülü 律呂); the pitch-pipes are the foundation of vocal and instrumental music. If one institutes music without using the pitch-pipes, how can one harmonize the measures of high and low, long and short, and keep them free from the faults of discord and encroachment? Understanding this, one may reply to a tiny fraction of Your enlightened question.

In antiquity, our Master, with his heaven-endowed sageliness, lived in the Spring and Autumn period and lamented the decay and loss of music. Taking the occasion of speaking about music to a music official of the time, he described a single musical movement (yicheng 一成) as "blended together (xiru 翕如), pure and harmonious (chunru 純如), clear and distinct (jiaoru 皦如), and flowing on continuously (yiru 繹如)." Mencius, who studied Confucius, in discussing the grand completion (dacheng 大成) of music, said "the bronze bell sounds it and the jade chime concludes it," which seems somewhat different. Yet if we examine the matter from within, even if the music is blended, pure, clear, and continuous, without the bronze bell to announce its sound at the beginning and the jade chime to gather in its resonance at the end, it certainly would not suffice to constitute a complete musical movement; and if the bronze bell sounds and the jade chime concludes, yet the music cannot be blended, pure, clear, and continuous, how then could it achieve musical harmony?

As for Mencius saying, "Without the six pitch-pipes (liulü 六律), one cannot rectify the five tones (wuyin 五音)," why is it that when the Master spoke of music to the Grand Music Master (Dashi 大師) of Lu, he did not mention the six pitch-pipes? It is because music becomes harmonious only through the six pitch-pipes; if it reaches the harmony of being blended, pure, clear, and continuous, it has never failed to come about through the six pitch-pipes. Therefore, although he did not explicitly speak of the six pitch-pipes, the six pitch-pipes are implied therein.

If we speak of them in terms of the Three Standards (santong 三統), then Yellow Bell (Huangzhong 黃鍾) is the Heaven Standard, Great Cluster (Taicu 太簇) is the Earth Standard, and Washing Clean (Guxian 姑洗) is the Man Standard—that is so. If we speak of them in terms of matching the twelve months, then Yellow Bell belongs to the firstbranch zi 子 [the eleventh month], Great Regulator (Dalü 大呂) belongs to chou 丑 [the twelfth month], Great Cluster belongs to yin 寅 [the first month], …

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
夾鍾属卯姑洗仲呂蕤賓林鍾則配之於辰巳午□
之月焉夷則南呂無射應鍾則配之於申酉戌亥之
月焉黄鍾至無射六律為陽大呂至應鍾六呂為陰
律以統氣類物呂以旅陽宣氣此陰陽取類之義也
六律皆旋相為宫隔八相生陽律生陰呂曰下生陰
呂生陽律曰上生上生者三分益一下生者三分損
一此損益相生之法也宫商角徵羽五聲者正聲也
商以前止有五聲至周加文武二聲謂之變宫變徵
君為宫徵為事君摠萬物不可執以一方事通萬務
===
不可滯於一隅此二聲所以有變也樂音最忌陵臣
如黄鍾為宫其律最長則餘律並用正聲固順若以
他律為宫則長短必有陵犯故但折用半律之聲方
能適均如以太簇為宫則大呂為徵而當用子聲者
是也黄鍾之管其長九寸空圍九分積八百一十分
以至宫聲八十一商聲七十二角聲六十四徵聲五
十四羽聲四十八變宫聲四十二變徵聲五十六此
正變全半之辨分寸度數之詳可考見者如此律呂
之說先儒議論皆未之合近世惟西山蔡氏通旁搜
alt_text:
夾鍾屬卯姑洗仲呂蕤賓林鍾則配之於辰巳午未
之月焉夷則南呂無射應鍾則配之於申酉戌亥之
月焉黃鍾至無射六律爲陽大呂至應鍾六呂爲陰
律以統氣類物呂以旅陽宣氣此陰陽取類之義也
六律皆旋相爲宮隔八相生陽律生陰呂曰下生陰
呂生陽律曰上生上生者三分益一下生者三分去
一此損益相生之法也宮商角徵羽五聲者正聲也
商以前止有五聲至周加文武二聲謂之變宮變之
君爲宮徵爲事君總萬物不可執以一方事適變而
===

之說歷代儒者辯論皆未之合近世惟西山蔡氏通旁搜
punctuated: 夾鍾属卯，姑洗、仲呂、蕤賓、林鍾則配之於辰、巳、午、□之月焉，夷則、南呂、無射、應鍾則配之於申、酉、戌、亥之月焉。黄鍾至無射六律為陽，大呂至應鍾六呂為陰。律以統氣類物，呂以旅陽宣氣，此陰陽取類之義也。六律皆旋相為宫，隔八相生。陽律生陰呂曰下生，陰呂生陽律曰上生。上生者三分益一，下生者三分損一，此損益相生之法也。宫、商、角、徵、羽五聲者，正聲也。商以前止有五聲，至周加文、武二聲，謂之變宫、變徵。君為宫，徵為事；君摠萬物，不可執以一方，事通萬務，不可滯於一隅，此二聲所以有變也。樂音最忌陵臣，如黄鍾為宫，其律最長，則餘律並用正聲，固順；若以他律為宫，則長短必有陵犯，故但折用半律之聲，方能適均，如以太簇為宫，則大呂為徵，而當用子聲者是也。黄鍾之管，其長九寸，空圍九分，積八百一十分；以至宫聲八十一、商聲七十二、角聲六十四、徵聲五十四、羽聲四十八、變宫聲四十二、變徵聲五十六：此正變全半之辨、分寸度數之詳，可考見者如此。律呂之說，先儒議論皆未之合，近世惟西山蔡氏通，旁搜
translation_en: …Jiazhong 夾鍾 belongs to mao 卯; Guxian 姑洗, Zhonglü 仲呂, Ruibin 蕤賓, and Linzhong 林鍾 are matched with the months of chen 辰, si 巳, wu 午, and [wei 未] □; and Yize 夷則, Nanlü 南呂, Wuyi 無射, and Yingzhong 應鍾 are matched with the months of shen 申, you 酉, xu 戌, and hai 亥. The six standard pitch-pipes (lü 律) from Huangzhong 黄鍾 to Wuyi are yang, while the six companion pitch-pipes (lü 呂) from Dalü 大呂 to Yingzhong are yin. The yang pitch-pipes統 govern the vital breaths (qi) and classify myriad things, whereas the yin pitch-pipes assist the yang in spreading the vital breaths; this is the meaning of their classification according to yin and yang. The pitch-pipes all take turns serving as the fundamental tone (gong 宫), generating one another at intervals of eight. When a yang pitch-pipe generates a yin pitch-pipe, it is called "downward generation" (xiasheng 下生); when a yin pitch-pipe generates a yang pitch-pipe, it is called "upward generation" (shangsheng 上生). Upward generation adds one-third to the length, while downward generation subtracts one-third; this is the method of mutual generation by subtraction and addition. The five tones—gong 宫, shang 商, jue 角, zhi 徵, and yu 羽—are the regular tones (zhengsheng 正聲). Before the Shang dynasty there were only five tones; by the Zhou dynasty, the two tones of Wen 文 and Wu 武 were added, called "altered gong" (biangong 變宫) and "altered zhi" (bianzhi 變徵). The ruler corresponds to gong, and affairs correspond to zhi. Because the ruler presides over all things and cannot be held to a single direction, and affairs encompass myriad duties and cannot be confined to a single corner, these two tones therefore have altered forms. In musical tones, what is most taboo is for a subordinate tone to encroach upon the ruler's tone [? 陵臣, for 臣陵]. For example, when Huangzhong serves as gong, since its pipe is the longest, all the other pitch-pipes can use their regular full-length tones and remain in proper order. If another pitch-pipe serves as gong, however, the relative lengths will inevitably result in encroachment and violation; therefore, one must halve the length and use the half-pipe tone (banlü 半律) in order to achieve proper balance. For instance, if Taicu 太簇 serves as gong, then Dalü serves as zhi, and ought to use its diminutive tone (zisheng 子聲). The tube of Huangzhong is nine cun 寸 in length, with an interior cross-sectional area of nine square fen 分 and a volume of eight hundred and ten cubic fen; and from this are derived the numbers eighty-one for the gong tone, seventy-two for the shang tone, sixty-four for the jue tone, fifty-four for the zhi tone, forty-eight for the yu tone, forty-two for the altered gong tone, and fifty-six for the altered zhi tone. Such are the distinctions between regular and altered, full and half tones, and the detailed measurements in fen and cun as they can be examined and seen. Regarding the theory of the pitch-pipes, the discussions of earlier Confucian scholars never reached agreement; in recent ages, only Master Cai of Xishan (Cai Yuanding 蔡元定) thoroughly… [? 通旁搜]

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
博采作律吕新書觀其黃鍾圍徑之數則漢斛之積
分可考寸以九分為法則淮南太史小司馬之說可
推以至先求聲氣之元而因律以生尺而亦雜見於
兩漢之制蔡邕之說故朱子稱其明白而淵深縝密
而通暢其言雖出於近世所未講而無一字不本於
古人已試之成法信有合於古矣至若司馬遷之序
律書其始不言律而言兵不言兵之用而言兵之偃
而於漢文尤加詳焉盖文帝偃兵息民結和通使而
天下安樂民氣歡洽陰陽協和天地之氣亦随以正
===
苟制律以候之以天地之正氣定一代之正律律有
不可定者乎司馬遷可謂知制律之時達制律之本
矣姑撫之以復明問
第四問
萬安
同考試官脩撰裴批塲中答此策者多敷衍問目是篇獨本
仁義立說有照應有斷制讀之令人竦然
考試官侍講杜批問目不遺折衷允當可取
考試官學士高批此答始終以周孔仁義為說其有識之士欤

博采作律呂新書觀其黃鍾圍徑之數則漢斛之積
分可考寸以九分爲法則淮南太史小司馬之說可

而於漢文尤加諄焉蓋文帝偃兵息民結和通使而
天下安樂民氣歡洽陰陽協和天地之氣亦隨以正
===
苟制律以候之以天地之正氣定一代之正律律有
不可定者乎司馬遷可謂知制律之時達制律之本
矣姑摭之以復明問
第四問
戴安
同考試官脩撰裴　批場中答此策者多敷衍問目是篇獨本
〔仁義立說有照應有斷制讀之令人竦然〕
考試官侍講杜　批問目不遺折衷允當可取
考試官學士高　批此答始終以周孔仁義爲說其有識之士歟
punctuated:
博采，作《律吕新書》。觀其黃鍾圍徑之數，則漢斛之積分可考；寸以九分為法，則淮南、太史、小司馬之說可推；以至先求聲氣之元，而因律以生尺，而亦雜見於兩漢之制、蔡邕之說。故朱子稱其「明白而淵深，縝密而通暢」，其言雖出於近世所未講，而無一字不本於古人已試之成法，信有合於古矣。至若司馬遷之序《律書》，其始不言律而言兵，不言兵之用而言兵之偃，而於漢文尤加詳焉。盖文帝偃兵息民，結和通使，而天下安樂，民氣歡洽，陰陽協和，天地之氣亦随以正。苟制律以候之，以天地之正氣定一代之正律，律有不可定者乎？司馬遷可謂知制律之時、達制律之本矣。姑撫之以復明問。

第四問
萬安
同考試官脩撰裴批：塲中答此策者，多敷衍問目，是篇獨本仁義立說，有照應，有斷制，讀之令人竦然。
考試官侍講杜批：問目不遺，折衷允當，可取。
考試官學士高批：此答始終以周、孔仁義為說，其有識之士欤！
translation_en:
…and gathered widely, composing the New Book of Pitch-Pipes (Lülü xinshu). When one examines his figures for the circumference and diameter of the Yellow Bell (huangzhong) pipe, the cumulative subdivisions of the Han standard dry measure (hu) can be verified; taking nine fen to the inch (cun) as the rule, the theories of the Prince of Huainan, the Grand Historian, and the Junior Sima [Sima Zhen] can be deduced; and as for first seeking the origin of sound and vital ether (qi) and thereby deriving the foot-measure from the pitch-pipe, this too appears scattered throughout the institutions of the Western and Eastern Han and the discussions of Cai Yong. Therefore Master Zhu [Zhu Xi] praised it as "clear yet profound, meticulous yet fluent," and remarked that although his words went beyond what recent ages had discussed, not a single character failed to be rooted in the established methods already tested by the ancients—truly, it was in accord with antiquity!

As for Sima Qian's preface to the "Treatise on Pitch-Pipes" (Lushu), at the outset it speaks not of pitch-pipes but of warfare, and not of the employment of arms but of the laying down of arms, dwelling in particular detail upon Emperor Wen of the Han. For Emperor Wen laid down arms and gave rest to the people, concluded peace and exchanged envoys, so that the realm enjoyed peace and happiness, the spirit of the people was joyful and harmonious, yin and yang were brought into accord, and the vital ether of Heaven and Earth likewise became rectified. If one were to fashion pitch-pipes to observe theether under such conditions—using the rectified ether of Heaven and Earth to fix the standard pitch-pipes of an era—how could the pitch-pipes fail to be fixed? Sima Qian may truly be said to have known the proper time for establishing pitch-pipes and understood the fundamental basis of establishing them. I tentatively gather these points in reply to the brilliant question.

Fourth Question
Wan An
Associate Examiner and Historiographer (xiuzhuan) Pei comments: Those in the examination compound who answered this policy question mostly did no more than elaborate mechanically on the topics of the prompt. This essay alone establishes its argument on the basis of benevolence and righteousness; it has structural coherence and decisive judgment, making one stand in awe upon reading it.
Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Du comments: None of the points in the question are omitted, and its balanced synthesis is sound and fitting. Acceptable.
Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Gao comments: From beginning to end, this answer grounds its argument in the benevolence and righteousness of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. Surely he is a scholar of true insight!

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
致治而用儒吏之臣者功業有不同為治而法周孔
之教者明驗有可必盖為治固當用儒吏之臣而尤
不可不法周孔仁義之教也不法周孔仁義之教則
又豈能措斯民於熈皡底斯世於隆平者乎此兩漢
所以止於漢而不能比隆於三代也歟且夫三代之
時君之所行皆仁義之道臣之所言亦皆仁義之道
是以治隆俗美有非後世所及也由兹而下称治之
善者必曰兩漢若髙帝之得天下其所以與治者率
多刀筆之吏儒者僅一二見焉當時若蕭何之填國
===
家撫百姓定畫一之法曹參則守而弗失載其清靜
民以寧一宜其功業為一時之冠有非他臣可比矣
然叔孫通以文學之臣制綿蕞之禮其功業不能與
蕭曹抗衡者豈非徒以禮儀之末僅能止武臣之喧
爭而不知以仁義之道賛其君也歟迨至文帝務崇
德化景帝處身恭儉致治之美庶幾成康論者謂其
皆尚黃老之所致殊不知當時所用之臣如周勃之
重厚萬石君之孝第賈誼之文學諫諍亦有助於其
間也武帝繼業罷黜百家表章六經而公孫弘之徒
alt_text:
致治而用儒吏之臣者功業有不同爲治而法周孔
之教者明驗有可必盖爲治固當用儒吏之臣而尤
不可不法周孔仁義之教也不法周孔仁義之教則
又豈能措斯民於熈皡底也世於隆平者乎此兩漢
所以止於漢而不能比隆於三代也歟且夫三代之
時君之所行皆仁義之道臣之所言亦皆仁義之道
是以治隆俗美有非後世所及也由茲而下称治之
善者必曰兩漢若高帝之得天下其所以與治者率
多刀筆之吏儒者僅一二見焉當時若蕭何之塡國
===
家撫百姓定畫一之法曹參則守而弗失載其清静
民以寧一宜其功業爲一時之冠有非他臣可比矣
然叔孫通以文學之臣制綿蕞之禮其功業不能與
蕭曹抗衡者豈非徒以禮儀之末僅能止武臣之喧
爭而不知以仁義之道賛其君也歟廹至文帝務崇
德化景帝履身恭儉致治之美庶幾成康論者謂其
皆尚黄老之所致殊不知當時所用之臣如周勃之
重厚萬石君之孝弟賈誼之文學諫諍亦有助於其
間也武帝繼業罷黜百家表章六經而公孫弘之徒
punctuated:
致治而用儒、吏之臣者，功業有不同；為治而法周、孔之教者，明驗有可必。盖為治固當用儒、吏之臣，而尤不可不法周、孔仁義之教也。不法周、孔仁義之教，則又豈能措斯民於熈皡，底斯世於隆平者乎？此兩漢所以止於漢，而不能比隆於三代也歟！

且夫三代之時，君之所行皆仁義之道，臣之所言亦皆仁義之道，是以治隆俗美，有非後世所及也。由兹而下，称治之善者，必曰兩漢。若髙帝之得天下，其所以與治者，率多刀筆之吏，儒者僅一二見焉。當時若蕭何之填國家、撫百姓、定畫一之法，曹參則守而弗失，載其清靜，民以寧一，宜其功業為一時之冠，有非他臣可比矣。然叔孫通以文學之臣，制綿蕞之禮，其功業不能與蕭、曹抗衡者，豈非徒以禮儀之末，僅能止武臣之喧爭，而不知以仁義之道賛其君也歟？迨至文帝務崇德化，景帝處身恭儉，致治之美，庶幾成、康。論者謂其皆尚黃、老之所致，殊不知當時所用之臣，如周勃之重厚、萬石君之孝第、賈誼之文學諫諍，亦有助於其間也。武帝繼業，罷黜百家，表章六經，而公孫弘之徒…
translation_en:
When seeking to bring about good governance by employing Confucian scholars and administrative clerks as ministers, their achievements and enterprises differ; when governing by taking the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius as the model, clear efficacy can be assured. Indeed, in governing one certainly ought to employ both Confucian scholars and administrative clerks as ministers, yet it is especially imperative to model oneself upon the teachings of benevolence and righteousness of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. If one does not model oneself upon the teachings of benevolence and righteousness of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, how then could one place this people in a state of serene contentment and bring this world to flourishing peace? Is this not why the Two Han dynasties remained merely the Han, and were unable to rival the splendor of the Three Dynasties?

Moreover, during the era of the Three Dynasties, what the ruler practiced was entirely the Way of benevolence and righteousness, and what the ministers spoke of was likewise entirely the Way of benevolence and righteousness; therefore, governance was flourishing and customs were admirable in a way that later ages could not match. From that time onward, those who praise excellence in governance invariably speak of the Two Han dynasties. When Emperor Gao (Gaodi) won the realm, those with whom he shared in governing were mostly scribes of the knife and brush, while Confucian scholars were seen in only one or two instances. At that time, someone like Xiao He pacified the state, comforted the common people, and established uniform laws, while Cao Can maintained them without fail; borne along by his tranquil non-interference, the people thereby found peace and unity. Rightly did their achievements top their age, beyond what any other ministers could compare to. Yet Shusun Tong, as a minister of literary learning, devised court ceremonial using ropes and bundled grass for rehearsal; that his achievements could not rival those of Xiao He and Cao Can—was it not because he merely used the superficialities of ritual decorum, managing only to halt the boisterous wrangling of military officers, without knowing how to assist his ruler with the Way of benevolence and righteousness? Coming down to Emperor Wen (Wendi), who devoted himself to exalting moral transformation, and Emperor Jing (Jingdi), who conducted himself with respectful frugality, the beauty of the governance they achieved nearly approached that of Kings Cheng and Kang of Zhou. Commentators claim that this was all brought about by their esteem for the doctrines of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi (Huang-Lao), scarcely realizing that the ministers employed at the time—such as Zhou Bo with his grave solidity, Lord Wanshi (Shi Fen) with his filial piety and fraternal submission, and Jia Yi with his literary learning and remonstrances—also contributed amidst it all. When Emperor Wu (Wudi) succeeded to the enterprise, he dismissed the Hundred Schools, exalted the Six Classics, and men of Gongsun Hong's ilk …

title: 正統十三年會試錄
text:
用事然治效不及夫文景豈非由公孫弘以曲學阿
世而不能止其好大喜功窮兵黷武之失乎宣帝中
興綜覈名實信賞必罰政事文學法理之士咸精其
能吏称其職民安其業功光祖宗業垂後裔侔德商
宗周宣可謂美矣要皆諸君勤勵之所致儒臣仁義之
所經濟也夫豈黃老之術刀筆之吏而致然哉雖然
為治固不可任夫刀筆又不可尚夫清浄必宗夫周
孔之教斯乃無弊焉且周孔之教仁義之言也前乎
已往後乎方来舉而行之皆有明驗愚也倘得進用
===
於時必為上為德非仁義之道不敢陳於
上為下為民非仁義之道不敢施諸下以求底於臯夔伊
尹周召之事業然後已也豈止於漢諸臣而已哉愚
生狂斐進而教之幸甚
第五問
同考試官教諭林批五策皆贍乾象一篇尤佳非博雅之
士不及此歆羨歆羨
考試官侍講杜批考據精詳筆力老健末以堯舜為説

能吏稱其職民安其業功光祖宗業垂後裔侔德商
宗周宣可謂羨矣要皆諸君勤勵之所致儒臣仁義之
所經濟也夫豈黃老之術刀筆之吏而致然哉雖然
為治固不可任夫刀筆又不可尚夫清淨必宗夫周
孔之教斯乃無弊焉且周孔之教仁義之言也前乎
已往後乎方來舉而行之皆有明驗愚也倘得進用
於時必為上為德非仁義之道不敢陳於
上為下為民非仁義之道不敢施諸下以求底於臯夔伊
尹周召之事業然後已也豈止於漢諸臣而已哉愚
生狂斐進而教之幸甚
第五問
同考試官教諭林　批五策皆貽黻象篇尤佳非博雅之
士不及此歆羨歆羨
考試官侍講杜　批考據精詳筆力老健末以堯舜為說
punctuated:
用事，然治效不及夫文、景，豈非由公孫弘以曲學阿世，而不能止其好大喜功、窮兵黷武之失乎？宣帝中興，綜覈名實，信賞必罰，政事、文學、法理之士咸精其能，吏称其職，民安其業，功光祖宗，業垂後裔，侔德商宗、周宣，可謂美矣。要皆諸君勤勵之所致，儒臣仁義之所經濟也，夫豈黃老之術、刀筆之吏而致然哉？雖然，為治固不可任夫刀筆，又不可尚夫清浄，必宗夫周、孔之教，斯乃無弊焉。且周、孔之教，仁義之言也，前乎已往，後乎方来，舉而行之，皆有明驗。愚也倘得進用於時，必為上為德，非仁義之道不敢陳於上；為下為民，非仁義之道不敢施諸下，以求底於臯、夔、伊尹、周、召之事業然後已也，豈止於漢諸臣而已哉！愚生狂斐，進而教之，幸甚。

第五問

同考試官教諭林批：五策皆贍，乾象一篇尤佳，非博雅之士不及此。歆羨，歆羨。
考試官侍講杜批：考據精詳，筆力老健，末以堯、舜為説，
translation_en:
…held power, yet the efficacy of the governance did not match that of Emperors Wen and Jing. Was this not because Gongsun Hong (公孫弘) used distorted learning to pander to the age and could not stop the Emperor's faults of delighting in grandiose achievements and exhausting the military in wanton warfare? When Emperor Xuan achieved a dynastic revival, he comprehensively verified names and realities, made rewards trustworthy and punishments certain, so that gentlemen of statecraft, literature, and legal principles all perfected their abilities, officials matched their offices, and the people were content in their livelihoods. His achievements brought glory to his ancestors, and his enterprise was handed down to his posterity; matching in virtue the high ancestors of Shang and King Xuan of Zhou, it may well be called splendid! In sum, all of this was brought about by the diligent exertion of those rulers and ordered by the benevolence and righteousness of Confucian ministers—how could it have been brought about by the arts of Huang-Lao or by petty scribes of the knife and brush? Even so, in governing one certainly must not rely upon petty scribes of the knife and brush, nor should one exalt quietistic purity; only when one takes as authoritative the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius will there be no defects. Moreover, the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are words of benevolence and righteousness. Looking back to the past and forward to the future, whenever they have been taken up and put into practice, there has always been clear verification. Should this foolish one gain advancement and employment in this age, in serving the sovereign and cultivating virtue, I would not dare to set before the sovereign anything that is not the Way of benevolence and righteousness; in serving below and caring for the people, I would not dare to apply to those below anything that is not the Way of benevolence and righteousness—seeking to attain to the achievements of Gao Yao (臯陶), Kui (夔), Yi Yin (伊尹), the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao before stopping! How could I stop merely at the various ministers of the Han! This foolish student is rash and unpolished; if I am advanced and instructed, I shall be most fortunate.

The Fifth Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Lin: All five policy essays are rich and ample, and the piece on celestial phenomena is especially fine; none but a gentleman of broad learning and refinement could reach this level. Admirable, admirable!
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Du: The evidential research is precise and detailed, the brushwork vigorous and mature, and at the end he bases his argument on Yao and Shun…

text:
為未能盡與巫咸甘石數家相合要亦不可不謂術
之精也若夫漢史所載十月五星聚東井之說此蓋
漢史欲神其事不復推之於理宜有以來允之所譏
也愚竊於終篇有獻焉夫垂象雖本於天道而觀象
則在於人心蓋以天觀天者不過技而已曷若以人
而觀天乎天象之高明即此心之高明天象之昭回
即此心之昭回堯有曆象羲和所能預而不知堯之
心自具一曆象也舜有璣衡七政所由齊而不知舜
之心自具一璣衡也後世之致治者要當以堯舜為
===
法管見如斯未知是否惟進而教之幸甚

為未能盡與巫咸、甘、石數家相合，要亦不可不謂術之精也。若夫漢史所載十月五星聚東井之說，此蓋漢史欲神其事，不復推之於理，宜有以來允之所譏也。

愚竊於終篇有獻焉。夫垂象雖本於天道，而觀象則在於人心。蓋以天觀天者，不過技而已，曷若以人而觀天乎？天象之高明，即此心之高明；天象之昭回，即此心之昭回。堯有曆象，羲、和所能預，而不知堯之心自具一曆象也；舜有璣衡，七政所由齊，而不知舜之心自具一璣衡也。後世之致治者，要當以堯、舜為法。管見如斯，未知是否？惟進而教之，幸甚。
translation_en:
…as failing to accord completely with the several schools of Wu Xian 巫咸, Gan De 甘德, and Shi Shen 石申, yet in essence one cannot but call it refined in its art. As for the account recorded in the Han histories that in the tenth month the Five Planets gathered in the Eastern Well (Dongjing 東井), this was merely because the Han historians wished to make the event seem miraculous and no longer investigated it according to principle; it is fitting that this drew the ridicule of Cui Yun 崔浩 [Allowing for the text's 來允 (Gao Yun 高允)].[?]

I humbly venture to offer a concluding thought at the end of this essay. Although the display of celestial signs is rooted in the Way of Heaven, the observation of those signs lies in the human mind. For observing Heaven by means of Heaven is nothing more than a technical skill; how can it compare to observing Heaven by means of the human? The lofty brilliance of the celestial signs is none other than the lofty brilliance of this mind; the radiant revolving of the celestial signs is none other than the radiant revolving of this mind. Yao 堯 had calendrical calculations of the celestial signs, in which Xi 羲 and He 和 were able to participate, yet people do not know that Yao's own mind naturally possessed its own calendrical calculations; Shun 舜 had the sighting tube and armillary sphere (jiheng 璣衡) by which the Seven Governors (qizheng 七政) wereordered, yet people do not know that Shun's own mind naturally possessed its own sighting tube and armillary sphere. Those in later generations who would bring about good governance ought essentially to take Yao and Shun as their model. Such is my humble view, though I do not know whether it is right or wrong; I only pray that I may be advanced and instructed, which would be most fortunate.

會試錄後序

《易》不云乎：「天地養萬物，聖人養賢以及萬民。」夫天地之間，品物庶類，覆載並育，無一不遂其生者，天地之仁也；四海之大，億兆之衆，撫綏匡直，使各安其生，囿於泰和之治者，聖人之仁也。聖人體天地之心，養賢以濟其仁；賢者體聖人之心，宣其仁以澤天下。故堯、舜之仁，不徧愛人，而必急親賢之為務也。洪惟我朝受天明命，奄有四海，養士以學校，而取之於科目。
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Does not the Book of Changes (Yi) say: "Heaven and earth nourish the myriad things; the sage nourishes the worthy in order to reach the myriad people"? Now, between heaven and earth, the various things and multitude of species are sheltered, borne up, and nurtured together so that not a single one fails to fulfill its life—this is the benevolence of heaven and earth. Throughout the vastness of the Four Seas and among the teeming millions of the populace, pacifying, comforting, rectifying, and straightening them so that each finds peace in their livelihood and is encompassed within a governance of great harmony—this is the benevolence of the sage. The sage embodies the mind of heaven and earth, nourishing the worthy in order to carry out his benevolence; the worthy embody the mind of the sage, spreading his benevolence to benefit all under heaven. Therefore, the benevolence of Yao and Shun did not consist in loving everyone indiscriminately, but necessarily took drawing close to the worthy as its urgent priority.

I humbly reflect that our Dynasty received the bright mandate of Heaven and came to possess all within the Four Seas, nourishing scholars through schools and selecting them through examination categories.

translation_en:
… As the successive sage emperors carried on the line, educational methods became ever more complete; worthy talents emerged in abundance, governance and moral transformation shone brightly, and the civilized and tribal peoples alike all submitted and obeyed. Since His Sacred Majesty succeeded to the Great Treasure of the throne, He has striven cautiously and diligently for good governance, daily attending the Classics Mat to continue and illuminate sacred learning, and visiting in person the Directorate of Education (chengjun) to perform the libation sacrifice to the Former Sage. The means by which He has cultivated and strengthened the source of moral transformation and inspired the community of scholars have reached the utmost! His earnest heart for nurturing the worthy is entirely for the sake of this people. Oh, how magnificent!

In the second month of spring of the wuchen year of the Zhengtong reign (1448), the Ministry of Rites held the Metropolitan Examination for tribute scholars (gongshi) from across the realm. The Minister [of Rites], Your Servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, petitioned for the appointment of Examiners, and His Majesty commanded Your Servant [Gao] Gu 高穀 and Your Servant [Du] Ning 杜寧 to go and oversee the affair. Thereupon, with pure and united hearts, we dared not slacken in the slightest, and obtained one hundred and fifty men whose compositions were of superior grade, compiling this into a brief record. translation_en: …formed through instruction, nurture, and molding. The Book of Odes (Shi) says: "Easy and self-possessed was our prince; did he not exert an influence upon men?" This speaks of King Wen's delight in bringing talent to maturity. It also says: "Stately are the many officers; through them King Wen enjoys repose." This speaks of the efficacy of the many officers in assisting governance. Now all you scholars, having been bathed in profound and generous grace and inspired by the transformative influence under which kites fly and fish leap, have had your names placed upon the roster of the worthies' examination, and will advance to reply at the Great Court, soon to receive illustrious promotion. The way in which you have been molded and brought to accomplishment is just like that of the many officers under King Wen. Why not reflect upon how to exhaust yourselves in repaying this? The worthies of antiquity wished to make their ruler like Yao and Shun and to bestow great enrichment upon the realm; if a single man failed to find his place, they regarded it as their own shame. May all you scholars take this as your own encouragement, so that through fine counsels and fine plans, good governance and good conduct, above you are able to benefit the state, and below to bring blessings to the common people.
